chapter.title: Design Google Drive
chapter.source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
chapter.primary_goal: Design a reliable, highly available, scalable cloud file storage and synchronization system supporting upload/download, multi-device synchronization, file revisions, sharing, notifications, strong metadata consistency, low bandwidth usage, and efficient storage.

chapter_summary.overview: Chapter 15 designs a Google Drive-like cloud storage system. The scoped product supports file upload and download, multi-device synchronization, revision history, file sharing, and notifications for edits, deletions, and shares. It supports web and mobile clients, any file type, encrypted storage, files up to 10 GB, and 10 million DAU. The non-functional requirements emphasize reliability, fast sync, bandwidth efficiency, scalability, and high availability. The chapter starts from a single-server architecture and evolves it into a distributed design using load balancers, horizontally scalable web/API servers, a replicated/sharded metadata database, object storage with cross-region replication, block servers, metadata caching, a notification service, and an offline backup queue. Files are split into blocks, compressed, encrypted, and uploaded to cloud storage. Delta sync sends only modified blocks. Strong consistency is required for metadata, so cache invalidation and relational ACID semantics are emphasized. Upload and download flows coordinate metadata changes with block transfer and notification delivery. Long polling is selected for notifications because updates are infrequent and mostly server-to-client. Storage is reduced through block-level deduplication, intelligent revision retention, and cold storage. The chapter closes with a failure-handling playbook and discusses the tradeoff between centralized block servers and direct client-to-cloud uploads.

important_features: Notify users when a file is edited, deleted, or shared
out_of_scope: Google Docs-style real-time collaborative document editing

non_functional_requirements.details: Slow synchronization can cause users to abandon the product.
Avoid unnecessary network use, especially for mobile users.
Remain usable despite slow/offline servers or network errors.

single_server_design.namespace_model: Each user has a namespace directory containing uploaded files. A file/folder can be uniquely identified by combining the namespace with its relative path.

types.resumable_upload: Use for large files or when network interruption is likely.

resumable_steps: Send initial request to retrieve a resumable URL.
Upload data and monitor upload state.

security.note: SSL protects data transfer between client and backend servers.

evolution_from_single_server.first_problem: Local storage fills up as more files are uploaded.
evolution_from_single_server.first_scaling_response: Shard storage across multiple servers, e.g. by user_id.
evolution_from_single_server.durability_concern: A storage-server outage can cause data loss/unavailability.
evolution_from_single_server.replication_goal: Store redundant files in multiple regions to guard against data loss and ensure availability.

distributed_improvements.improvement: Evenly distribute traffic and reroute traffic if a web server fails.
Add/remove servers easily based on traffic load.
Move off the web server, replicate and shard to eliminate the single point of failure and improve scale.
Use S3 and replicate files in two separate geographic regions.

sync_conflicts.when_conflict_occurs: Two users modify the same file or folder at the same time.
sync_conflicts.resolution_rule: The first version processed wins; the later version receives a conflict.
sync_conflicts.user_experience: Present both the user's local copy and the latest server version. The user can merge the files or override one version with the other.

high_level_design_components.role: Uses the product from a browser or mobile application.
Upload file blocks to cloud storage. Split files into blocks; each block has a unique hash and is an independent object. Reconstruct files by joining blocks in order.
Stores inactive data that has not been accessed for a long time.
Evenly distributes requests among API servers.
Handle nearly everything except the upload flow: authentication, profiles, metadata updates, etc.
Stores user, file, block, version, and related metadata; actual file contents stay in cloud storage.
Caches some metadata for fast retrieval.
Publisher/subscriber service that notifies clients when files are added, edited, or removed elsewhere so clients can pull the latest changes.
Stores change information for offline clients until they reconnect.

block_server_design.problem: Sending an entire large file after every edit consumes excessive bandwidth.

optimizations.name: Delta sync
optimizations.details: Transfer only modified blocks rather than the whole file.

optimizations.name: Compression
optimizations.details: Compress blocks before upload. Compression algorithm depends on file type; gzip and bzip2 are examples for text files.

consistency_model.reason: It is unacceptable for different clients to see different versions of a file at the same time.
cache_requirements: Keep cache replicas consistent with the master.
consistency_model.nosql_note: NoSQL systems do not provide ACID by default in the chapter's framing, so synchronization logic would need to add the required guarantees programmatically.

metadata_schema.purpose: Basic information such as username, email, and profile photo.
Device information; push_id supports mobile push notifications. One user may have multiple devices.
Everything related to the latest file state.
File revision history. Existing rows are read-only to preserve integrity.
File-block metadata. Any file version can be reconstructed by joining blocks in correct order.

parallel_requests: Upload file content to cloud storage
metadata_branch: Client sends request to add new-file metadata.
Store metadata in Metadata DB and mark upload status as pending.
Notify Notification Service that a new file is being added.
Notification Service informs relevant clients that a file is being uploaded.
content_branch: Client uploads file content to Block Servers.
Block Servers split, compress, encrypt, and upload blocks to cloud storage.
Cloud storage triggers an upload-completion callback to API servers.
API servers change file status to uploaded in Metadata DB.
Notify Notification Service that file status is uploaded.
Notification Service informs relevant clients that the file is fully uploaded.
upload_flow.edit_flow_note: Editing a file follows a similar flow.

download_flow.trigger: A file is added or edited elsewhere.
download_flow.online_client: Notification Service informs the online client that changes exist.
download_flow.offline_client: Change data is saved and the client pulls latest changes when it reconnects.
steps: Notification Service tells client that a file changed.
API servers fetch metadata from Metadata DB.
Metadata returns through API servers to client.
Client requests blocks from Block Servers.
Block Servers fetch blocks from cloud storage.
Cloud storage returns blocks to Block Servers.
Client downloads new blocks and reconstructs the file.

notification_service.purpose: Inform other clients about file mutations so they can pull latest changes and reduce conflicts.
reasons: Notification communication is not bidirectional; server sends change information to client.
Notifications are infrequent and do not arrive in large bursts.
WebSocket is more suitable for real-time bidirectional communication such as chat.
notification_service.long_poll_behavior: Each client keeps a long-poll connection open. When a file change is detected, the connection closes, the client fetches latest metadata/changes, then immediately opens a new long-poll request after receiving a response or reaching timeout.

storage_space_optimization.why_needed: Revision history and replication across data centers create many copies and can fill storage rapidly.

techniques.name: Block-level deduplication
techniques.details: Remove duplicate blocks at the account level; equal hashes indicate identical blocks.

techniques.name: Limit number of file versions
techniques.details: When the revision limit is reached, replace the oldest version with the newest.

techniques.name: Keep valuable versions only
techniques.details: For frequently edited files, retain fewer revisions and give more weight to recent versions.

techniques.name: Cold storage
techniques.details: Move data inactive for months or years to cheaper cold storage such as Amazon S3 Glacier.

failure_handling.recovery: Secondary load balancer becomes active. Load balancers monitor each other with heartbeat signals.
Other block servers pick up unfinished or pending jobs.
Fetch files from replicated copies in other regions.
Load balancer redirects traffic to another stateless API server.
Read from other replicated cache nodes and bring up a replacement node.
Promote a slave to become the new master and add a new slave.
Use another slave for reads and bring up a replacement DB server.
Clients lose long-poll connections and reconnect to another notification server. Reconnecting a very large number of clients can be slow.
Queues are replicated; consumers may re-subscribe to a backup queue.

wrap_up_tradeoffs.design_summary: The design combines strong consistency, low network bandwidth, fast synchronization, metadata management, file sync, and long-poll notifications.

direct_client_to_cloud_alternative.advantage: Faster upload because the file is transferred only once, directly from client to cloud storage.
drawbacks: Chunking, compression, and encryption logic must be implemented separately on iOS, Android, and web.
Duplicated client-side logic is error-prone and requires substantial engineering effort.
Client devices are easier to manipulate, so client-side encryption logic is not ideal.
direct_client_to_cloud_alternative.chapter_design_advantage: Centralized block servers keep chunking, compression, and encryption logic in one controlled place.

wrap_up_tradeoffs.possible_evolution: Move online/offline logic into a separate presence service so other services can reuse it.

key_concepts.definition: A user's root directory; combined with relative path to uniquely identify files/folders.
Upload method that can resume after interruption instead of restarting the entire transfer.
Service that splits, compresses, encrypts, and uploads file blocks.
Unique hash associated with a block; also used to detect identical blocks for deduplication.
Synchronize only modified blocks instead of transferring the entire file.
All clients should observe the same file/metadata state at the same time.
Invalidate metadata cache entries when the database is written so cache and DB stay aligned.
Read-only revision-history rows used to preserve file history integrity.
Pub/sub service that informs clients of file changes so they can pull updates.
Stores update information for clients that are offline.
Client holds a request open until change/timeout, then reconnects after fetching updates.
Save storage by eliminating identical blocks with the same hash.
Low-cost storage for data inactive for months or years.
Optional separate service for reusable online/offline state management.

scenario_questions.scenario: A 9 GB upload on a flaky mobile connection drops halfway through.
scenario_questions.question: Which upload mode should be used and why?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Resumable upload, so the transfer can continue rather than restart.

scenario_questions.scenario: A single local storage server is nearly full.
scenario_questions.question: What progression does the chapter use?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: First shard storage across servers, then adopt S3/object storage with replication for scalability and durability.

scenario_questions.scenario: Two users save different versions of the same file at the same time.
scenario_questions.question: How does the chapter resolve it?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: First processed version wins; the later writer gets a conflict and sees local plus latest server copies for merge/override.

scenario_questions.scenario: A 2 GB file changes only in two 4 MB regions.
scenario_questions.question: What optimization prevents retransmitting the whole file?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Delta sync sends only the modified blocks.

scenario_questions.scenario: Mobile bandwidth usage is too high for text-heavy files.
scenario_questions.question: Which block-server optimization helps?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Compression, using an algorithm appropriate for the file type such as gzip/bzip2 for text.

scenario_questions.scenario: Two metadata cache replicas disagree immediately after a file update.
scenario_questions.question: Which requirement is violated and how does the chapter address it?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Strong consistency is violated; keep replicas/master consistent and invalidate cache on DB writes.

scenario_questions.question: Which table behavior is relevant?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Existing File_version rows are read-only to preserve revision-history integrity.

scenario_questions.scenario: A client starts uploading a new file while another device is online.
scenario_questions.question: What does the metadata branch do?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Store metadata as pending, notify Notification Service, and inform relevant clients that a file is being uploaded.

scenario_questions.scenario: The same client finishes uploading all blocks.
scenario_questions.question: What completion path follows?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Cloud storage callback -> API server -> mark metadata uploaded -> notify Notification Service -> notify relevant clients.

scenario_questions.scenario: A user comes back online after another device edited a file.
scenario_questions.question: How does it catch up?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Stored change information allows it to pull latest metadata and changed blocks after reconnecting.

scenario_questions.scenario: You are choosing between WebSocket and long polling for Drive notifications.
scenario_questions.question: Why does the chapter choose long polling?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Traffic is infrequent and mostly server-to-client rather than persistent bidirectional communication.

scenario_questions.scenario: A heavily edited file produces thousands of versions.
scenario_questions.question: How can storage be controlled?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Set a revision limit and/or keep only valuable versions with preference for recent revisions.

scenario_questions.scenario: Years-old file versions are almost never accessed.
scenario_questions.question: Where should they move?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Cold storage such as S3 Glacier.

scenario_questions.scenario: A notification server holding many long-poll clients dies.
scenario_questions.question: What operational problem occurs?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Clients must reconnect elsewhere, but restoring a huge number of connections cannot happen instantly and is relatively slow.

scenario_questions.scenario: You propose uploading directly from client to cloud storage.
scenario_questions.question: What are the chapter's tradeoffs?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Faster one-hop upload, but chunking/compression/encryption logic must be duplicated across client platforms and client-side security is less trusted.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is a cloud-drive system more than simple file storage?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: It must reliably synchronize versions across devices, notify users of changes, manage conflicts and revisions, minimize bandwidth, and remain strongly consistent and highly available.

short_answer_questions.question: How does the architecture evolve from one server to a scalable system?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Start with web server + DB + local storage, then shard storage, move files to replicated object storage, add a load balancer and scalable web/API tier, and separate/replicate/shard the metadata database.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain block servers.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: They split files into blocks, compress and encrypt the blocks, upload them to cloud storage, and support delta sync so only modified blocks are transferred.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is strong consistency required and how is it maintained?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Different clients must not see different file states. The chapter requires cache replicas/master consistency and cache invalidation on DB writes, and chooses a relational DB because ACID is native.

short_answer_questions.question: Describe the upload flow.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Metadata and file-content requests run in parallel. Metadata is stored as pending and clients are notified; file content goes through block servers to cloud storage; a completion callback marks it uploaded and triggers another notification.

short_answer_questions.question: Describe the download/sync flow.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Notification Service tells a client about a change; the client fetches metadata through API servers, then requests blocks from Block Servers, which fetch them from cloud storage; the client downloads new blocks and reconstructs the file.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is long polling preferred over WebSocket?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Drive notifications are infrequent and essentially one-way; WebSocket's persistent bidirectional communication is more appropriate for chat-like workloads.

short_answer_questions.question: How does the design reduce storage space?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Deduplicate equal-hash blocks, limit/curate revision history with preference for recent versions, and move inactive data to cheaper cold storage.

short_answer_questions.question: What failure-handling patterns appear repeatedly?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Heartbeat failover, stateless rerouting, replicated storage/cache/queues, takeover by peer workers, and database replica promotion.

short_answer_questions.question: What is the block-server vs direct-client-upload tradeoff?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Direct upload is faster because data moves once, but processing/security logic must be duplicated on every client. Block servers add a hop but centralize chunking, compression, and encryption.

interview_style_questions.question: What requirements would you clarify for a cloud drive?
How would you evolve from a single server?
How would you reduce synchronization bandwidth?
How would you guarantee metadata consistency?
What protocol would you use for change notifications?
How would you reduce storage cost?
How would you handle component failures?
Would you upload directly from client to cloud storage?

common_confusions.confusion: Google Drive design is mostly about storing file bytes.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter emphasizes synchronization, revisions, notifications, conflicts, bandwidth, consistency, and reliability in addition to storage.

common_confusions.confusion: Metadata DB should contain the actual files.
common_confusions.correction: File contents live in cloud storage; Metadata DB stores metadata only.

common_confusions.confusion: Every edit should re-upload the whole file.
common_confusions.correction: Delta sync sends only modified blocks.

common_confusions.confusion: Block compression is identical for every file type.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter says compression algorithm should depend on file type.

common_confusions.confusion: Eventual consistency is acceptable for metadata because caches are fast.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter explicitly requires strong consistency for metadata cache and DB.

common_confusions.confusion: WebSocket must be better because it is more real time.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter chooses long polling because Drive notifications are infrequent and mostly one-way.

common_confusions.confusion: File revision history should always retain every revision forever.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter recommends limits/valuable-version policies to control storage use.

common_confusions.confusion: Direct client-to-cloud upload is strictly superior.
common_confusions.correction: It is faster, but duplicates processing/security logic across clients and moves sensitive logic onto less-trusted clients.

practice_problems.prompt: If signed-up users doubled to 100 million at 10 GB free each, what total allocated storage would that imply?
practice_problems.note: Derived from the chapter's allocation method.

practice_problems.prompt: If DAU doubled to 20 million with 2 uploads/day, estimate average upload QPS.
practice_problems.note: Derived by doubling the chapter's ~240 QPS.

practice_problems.prompt: A 100-block file changes in only blocks 2 and 5. How many blocks need uploading under delta sync?
User A's update is processed before User B's simultaneous update. What happens?
practice_problems.solution: User A's version wins; User B receives a conflict and is shown local and server copies.

practice_problems.prompt: Metadata DB is updated but stale cache remains. What must happen?
practice_problems.solution: Invalidate the cache entry so cache and DB reflect the same value.

practice_problems.prompt: Two account-level blocks have identical hashes. What optimization applies?
practice_problems.solution: Deduplicate them and store one copy/reference rather than redundant blocks.

practice_problems.prompt: A Drive-style notification channel is one-way and rarely active. Which protocol does the chapter choose?
The Metadata DB master fails while a slave is healthy. What should happen?
practice_problems.solution: Promote a slave to master and bring up a new slave.

beginner: Can state all functional and non-functional requirements.
Can reproduce 500 PB, 240 QPS, and 480 peak QPS.
Can explain simple vs resumable upload.
intermediate: Can explain evolution from one server to S3-based distributed design.
Can describe block-level storage, delta sync, compression, and encryption.
Can explain strong metadata consistency and relational ACID choice.
advanced: Can walk through every failure scenario.
Can defend centralized block servers vs direct client-to-cloud upload.
Can explain how notification and offline synchronization interact.
Can redraw the major chapter diagrams from memory.

must_memorize: Scope: upload/download, sync, revisions, share, notifications; no live Docs collaboration.
Clients: web + mobile; any file type; encrypted storage; max 10 GB; 10M DAU.
NFRs: reliability, fast sync, bandwidth efficiency, scalability, high availability.
Capacity: 50M users × 10 GB = 500 PB; upload ~240 QPS; peak 480.
APIs: upload, download, revisions; simple vs resumable; HTTPS.
Single server evolves to sharded storage, S3, load balancer, scalable web/API, replicated/sharded metadata DB.
Cross-region replication protects against data loss and improves availability.
Conflict rule: first processed version wins; later user sees local/server copies.
Block servers split, compress, encrypt, and upload blocks.
Dropbox reference block size = max 4 MB.
Delta sync sends only modified blocks.
Metadata requires strong consistency.
Invalidate metadata cache on DB writes.
Relational DB chosen because ACID is native.
Schema: User, Device, Namespace, File, File_version, Block.
Upload has parallel metadata and content branches.
File states: pending -> uploaded.
Download: notification -> metadata -> block download -> reconstruct.
Long polling selected over WebSocket for infrequent one-way notifications.
Save space with block dedup, revision limits/valuable versions, and cold storage.
Failures: heartbeat LB failover, block-server takeover, multi-region storage, stateless API reroute, cache replicas, DB promotion, notification reconnect, queue replicas.
Direct client-to-cloud upload is faster but duplicates client logic and weakens trust boundary.
Possible evolution: separate presence service.
chapter_fifteen_final_review.memory_chain: REQUIREMENTS -> CAPACITY -> SINGLE SERVER -> RESUMABLE APIs -> SHARD STORAGE -> S3 REPLICATION -> LB/API/METADATA -> CONFLICTS -> BLOCK SERVERS -> DELTA SYNC/COMPRESSION/ENCRYPTION -> STRONG CONSISTENCY -> SCHEMA -> PARALLEL UPLOAD -> DOWNLOAD SYNC -> LONG POLL -> DEDUP/VERSIONS/COLD STORAGE -> FAILURE HANDLING -> DIRECT-UPLOAD TRADEOFF
chapter_fifteen_final_review.one_sentence_takeaway: A scalable cloud drive combines strongly consistent metadata with block-level, bandwidth-efficient file synchronization, replicated object storage, long-poll change notifications, revision management, and robust failure recovery.
